title: FluentValidation (complex rules and testability)
hook: FluentValidation moves validation rules out of DTO attributes into dedicated, testable validator classes with a fluent API. It is the standard choice when data annotations become unreadable or you need async database checks.

blocks.text: FluentValidation is a popular open-source library that defines rules in AbstractValidator<T> classes using a chainable API — RuleFor, Must, When, and WithMessage. Rules live separately from DTOs, which keeps models as plain records and makes unit testing validation without HTTP context straightforward. The FluentValidation.AspNetCore integration registers validators in dependency injection and plugs into the same ModelState pipeline as data annotations, producing the same ValidationProblemDetails 400 responses for [ApiController] apps.

entries.plainDefinition: Base class where you define validation rules for type T in the constructor.
Selects a property and attaches validators like NotEmpty, EmailAddress, or custom Must predicates.
FluentValidation service interface; Validate or ValidateAsync returns ValidationResult with errors.
Auto-validation filter runs all registered IValidator<T> for action parameters before the action executes.

blocks.text: Real APIs accumulate conditional rules: password strength depends on account type, dates depend on timezone, SKUs depend on catalog version. Cramming that into attributes produces unmaintainable DTOs. FluentValidation supports dependent rules, collections, async MustAsync for database lookups, and clear error messages per rule. Interviewers expect you to know when FluentValidation beats annotations and how to test validators in isolation with TestValidate.

blocks.title: Keep DTOs thin
blocks.body: DTOs carry data; validators carry rules. Duplicate rules in both annotations and FluentValidation causes double errors — pick one strategy per DTO.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Auto-validation filter runs
items.body: Before the action, FluentValidation resolves IValidator<T> for each parameter and runs ValidateAsync.

items.title: Errors merge into ModelState
items.body: Property names map to ModelState keys; action short-circuits with 400 like annotation failures.

items.title: Action executes only when valid
items.body: Same ValidationProblemDetails shape clients expect from data annotations.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Registering both data annotations and FluentValidation on the same properties — duplicate errors in ModelState. Using MustAsync without cancellation token — request abort does not cancel DB lookup. Forgetting AddFluentValidationAutoValidation — validators registered but never invoked. Resolving scoped DbContext in validator registered as singleton — use IValidator with scoped lifetime via DI.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: validators with MustAsync add latency to every POST — track p95 validation duration in OpenTelemetry spans around the filter. Cache negative uniqueness checks carefully or you leak existence information. FluentValidation 11+ split packages: FluentValidation.DependencyInjectionExtensions for AddValidatorsFromAssembly. For high-throughput APIs, consider validating only at domain boundaries and using annotations for trivial shape checks — full FluentValidation on every field has a cost. Interviewers ask how you avoid N+1 in validators that hit the database per property.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Same 400 shape as annotations on controllers
Does not apply to minimal APIs by default
Must attach per route or convention
Not a substitute for input sanitization

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying FluentValidation replaces all domain validation — it validates input DTOs, not aggregate invariants. Unable to test validators without spinning up WebApplicationFactory. Putting DbContext in validator constructor on singleton registration. Not knowing minimal APIs need IEndpointFilter for the same behavior.

interviewTakeaways: FluentValidation puts rules in AbstractValidator<T> classes — testable, async-capable, separate from DTOs.
When not to use: trivial two-field DTOs where annotations suffice; avoid duplicate annotation + FV rules.
Production tip: span MustAsync DB calls; watch p95 on POST endpoints with uniqueness validators.

60s: Register AddValidatorsFromAssembly and auto-validation for controllers. Validators use RuleFor and MustAsync. Test with TestValidate. Minimal APIs need ValidationFilter IEndpointFilter. DTOs stay thin.
Follow-up: how do you share one validator between minimal APIs and MediatR handlers?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'FluentValidation runs automatically on MapPost' gets you rejected — only controller auto-validation unless you add endpoint filters.
Duplicate [Required] on DTO plus RuleFor NotEmpty — clients see two errors per field.

Strong answer: 'Validators in separate classes, registered in DI, tested with TestValidate. Controllers via auto-validation; minimal APIs via IEndpointFilter. Async uniqueness in MustAsync with cancellation. Domain rules stay in entities.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS global ValidationPipe mirrors FluentValidation auto-validation — decorators on DTO vs separate validator classes. FluentValidation's separation is cleaner for large rule sets and unit tests.
Joi.validate() in Express handlers is the manual equivalent of calling IValidator.Validate in an endpoint filter. Both produce field-keyed error maps for 400 responses.
